title: When would you use event-driven communication between services?
description: Events vs commands, pub/sub decoupling, eventual consistency, ordering and replay, and the operational costs of async architectures.

data.text: **Question:** When would you use event-driven communication between services?

Use events when **multiple consumers care about something that happened** and **the producer shouldn't know or wait for them**: order placed → inventory reserves, email sends, analytics records, search index updates. Events decouple producers from consumers in time and topology — the producer publishes and moves on; consumers join, leave, and lag independently. Use **synchronous request/reply** when the caller needs the answer now (auth check, read-your-write, validation). The costs you accept with events: **eventual consistency**, **at-least-once delivery semantics** (so consumers must be idempotent), and **operational complexity** — brokers, schema evolution, replay, and monitoring become production infrastructure.

**Events vs commands — the key distinction:**
- An **event** is a fact in past tense ('OrderPlaced'): any number of interested consumers; the producer has no expectations
- A **command** ('SendRefundEmail') has exactly one intended consumer and implies intent — closer to async RPC
- Publishing domain events from the service layer keeps business language in the integration ('PaymentCaptured', 'SubscriptionUpgraded')

**Patterns built on events:**
- **Pub/sub fan-out**: one publish, N independent consumers — the core decoupling win
- **CQRS**: events feed read-model projections; queries hit fast local stores
- **Event-carried state transfer**: the event carries the data consumers need, so they avoid calling back to the producer ('shadow copy' of state)
- **Saga choreography**: services react to each other's events without a central coordinator
- **Stream processing**: events as a durable log enable replay, time-travel debugging, and new consumers added retroactively

**Delivery semantics (know them cold):**
- Brokers give **at-least-once** (Kafka, SQS standard) — duplicates happen (retries, rebalances); consumers must be idempotent (dedupe keys, natural idempotency)
- **Exactly-once** is a processing property (Kafka transactions, idempotent producers), not a magic delivery mode — end-to-end exactly-once still requires idempotent side effects
- **Ordering**: guaranteed per partition/key (Kafka) — design keys so related events share a partition; global order is essentially unobtainable

**When NOT to use events:**
- The caller needs an immediate authoritative answer (payments auth, permission checks)
- Workflows where the user waits — async round trips make UX worse
- Small teams without ops capacity for a broker — request/reply between two services is fine at first

**Operational bill:** schema registry + backward/forward-compatible evolution, consumer lag monitoring, dead-letter queues, replay tooling, and tracing across async boundaries (correlation ids).

data.title: Order flow: sync for the answer, events for the fallout
data.code:
POST /orders  (user is waiting - synchronous where it matters)
  OrderService.PlaceOrder()
    - validate payment synchronously with PaymentService (need the answer NOW)
    - persist Order (status=Placed)
    - publish OrderPlaced event, commit, return 201

Event consumers (fire-and-forget fallout, each decoupled):
  InventoryService   -> reserve stock, publish StockReserved
  NotificationService-> confirmation email
  SearchService      -> index the product purchase history
  AnalyticsService   -> append to revenue stream
  LoyaltyService     -> award points

Adding 'award points' later = adding a consumer. Zero changes to OrderService.
That is the decoupling event-driven architecture buys.

Failure handling in the flow:
  Inventory can't reserve -> publishes OrderRejected
  NotificationService reacts to OrderRejected -> apologetic email
  (choreographed compensation - see sagas lesson)

Idempotent consumer sketch:
  on OrderPlaced(event):
    if processedEvents.contains(event.eventId): return  // dedupe
    reserve(event); processedEvents.add(event.eventId)

data.title: Events trade consistency for independence
data.text: After OrderPlaced, inventory, search, and analytics are each momentarily wrong until their consumers catch up. Design for that: show 'processing' states, tolerate stale reads, and never build user-visible flows that assume an event has already been consumed.

items: Publishing events consumers must have for the request to be correct — that's a sync call wearing a costume
Non-idempotent consumers with at-least-once delivery — duplicated emails and double charges
Events carrying no payload, forcing every consumer to call back to the producer
Ignoring consumer lag and DLQ monitoring — silent async failures
Global-order expectations — design partition keys instead
Choreography spaghetti: 12 consumers reacting to 12 events with no one able to explain the flow (consider orchestrated sagas)
How do you evolve an event schema without breaking existing consumers?
How does a consumer replay a backlog after a bugfix?
Choreography vs orchestration — when does each sag?
How do correlation ids stitch async traces together?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Events = facts with many interested consumers; commands = one intended consumer
Fan-out, CQRS projections, event-carried state, and sagas all build on events
At-least-once + idempotent consumers is the realistic contract
You pay with eventual consistency and broker operations — budget for both
data.takeaway: Publish events for the fallout of a business fact; call synchronously only when you genuinely need the answer before you can finish.
